action: Plan step 2, residue of the parameter-range kind, entry actions 1-4. Action 1, the finite version with its parameter: for each rank r >= 3 let KTT(r) be the statement that every triple of partitions with at most r parts each has a stretched Littlewood-Richardson polynomial with nonnegative coefficients. The parameter is the rank r, not the size: the size is already free inside each KTT(r). No constant has to be kept uniform, because the target is a decision. Action 2, the equivalence: KTT holds if and only if KTT(r) holds for every r, since every triple has finitely many parts, and KTT(r+1) implies KTT(r), so the family is a monotone exhaustion; and each KTT(r) is a finite statement, by either of two finitisations in print. (i) Local formula: for a period-one hive polytope the coefficient of t^{D-q} is the sum over the faces of codimension q of the lattice volume of the face times a weight depending only on the face's transverse cone (Berline-Vergne, McMullen; transferred to the rational hive polytope by Ferudun's period-one dilation lemma), and every transverse cone of a hive of rank r is generated by a subset of the fixed finite normal set N_r of primitive rhombus normals, which for r = 5 has 27 elements, so nonnegativity of every coefficient of every hive of rank r follows from nonnegativity of the weight on the finitely many cone types of N_r, one finite list per codimension. (ii) Chamber-wise: by Rassart the coefficient of t^k is a polynomial homogeneous of degree k on each of the finitely many chambers of the Littlewood-Richardson chamber complex of rank r, so KTT(r) is a finite list of polynomial-nonnegativity statements on rational cones, and for k = 1 the polynomial is linear and the statement is decided at the finitely many extreme rays of the chambers. Action 3, the side with a finite certificate: for each rank the true side has one, a nonnegative weight assignment on the rank-r cone atlas, which is the rank-r instance of Ferudun's (HTE); the false side has one globally, a single triple with its polynomial. Action 4: the residue is passed rank by rank. KTT(3) is trivial (dim H <= 1) and KTT(4) is a theorem (Ferudun 2026, Theorem 1), so the residue is R = {KTT(r) : r >= 5}, and its first member is handed to the child attack ktt-positivity-length-five, opened for this move.
output: The residue R = {KTT(r) : r >= 5}: the claim holds if and only if every member holds, each member is a finite statement, and the number of members is infinite, so this finitisation does not finitise the claim; what it gives is that each rung is decidable in principle and that a rung is a statement about all sizes at a fixed rank. The content of the first open rung is exactly two finite lists, both named in print as what is left after Ferudun's theorems: (a) the linear coefficient of full-dimensional five-part hives, which is localised at codimension five, so it needs the weight on five-dimensional transverse cones spanned by the 27 rank-five rhombus normals, that is on the C(27, 5) = 80,730 five-normal tuples and their closures; (b) the non-full-dimensional five-part hives of intrinsic dimension at least three, whose transverse cones are projections of N_5 and which the published atlas does not cover, and which Horn factorisation does not reduce to four parts (the example lam = (4,3,3,1), mu = (4,2,1,1), nu = (6,5,4,2,2) has dim H = 3 with all 142 essential Horn inequalities strict). Deduction back to the claim: proving KTT(5) gives the conjecture for every triple of length at most five at every size, extending the length <= 4 theorem by one rung, and leaves every rank r >= 6 open. Obligation the record owes: the finitisation of KTT(r) is complete for full-dimensional hives, where the transverse cones are generated by N_r itself; for the non-full-dimensional hives it needs the intrinsic-lattice contraction that turns a projected cone into a cone of the intrinsic lattice, which is stated as missing in the source and is part of list (b).

action: A derivation with no computation in it, written to study/rank-uniformity.md, auditing the child attack's results for dependence on the rank. Five statements proved there are statements about a rational polytope and its lattice and use no rank: the cell reduction, which makes the coefficient a linear functional on a cell so that nonnegativity on the whole cell is decided at its extreme rays; the nonnegative-class lemma; the disjointness of shares that makes a local domination statement sufficient; the per-facet identity, whose shares sum to the functional exactly; and the intrinsic-lattice contraction that turns a non-full-dimensional hive into the same problem one dimension lower. What is not rank-uniform is the atlas: transverse cones are generated by subsets of the normal set N_n, so the codimension-five list built at rank five is of no use at any other rank. Writing D(n) = (n-1)(n-2)/2 for the number of interior entries, the row construction gives |N_n| at most 3n(n-1)/2, which is 30 against the true 27 at n = 5.
output: The rungs get harder, not merely bigger, and the rank-five method is not a plan for the ladder. Ferudun's theorem gives the top four coefficients at every rank and a_0 is 1, so a full-dimensional hive of side n leaves a_1 up to a_{D(n)-4} open, that is D(n)-4 coefficients, and the coefficient a_k needs weights of transverse cones of codimension D(n)-k, so the codimensions run up to D(n)-1. That is no open coefficient at n = 4; two at n = 5, of which a_2 is settled by the rank-five codimension-four computation, leaving one coefficient and codimension five; six at n = 6, codimensions four to nine in a ten-dimensional space; eleven at n = 7. So the data the reductions consume grows quadratically in the rank in both the number of coefficients and the codimension, and no closed formula for the weights exists above dimension three. The consequence for the root is exact: the five reductions carry over to every rank unchanged, which makes a rank-uniform proof of the per-facet inequality a meaningful target, but repeating the rank-five computation rung by rung is not a route to the objective. The derivation proves no coefficient nonnegative at any rank.

action: A step into a second strategy, after the finite-computation route's own move 2 showed that repeating the rank-five atlas rung by rung is not a plan for the ladder. Step 1 of the strategy, the study, is study/reduce-and-translate.md: three queries on 2026-09-05, one of which, h* vector together with Littlewood-Richardson, returned nothing, so the destination language has not been pointed at this statement. Then the translation itself, derived in study/h-star-translation.md with no computation in it. Writing the polynomial in the binomial basis, P(t) = sum of h_i times C(t + d - i, d), which is possible for any polynomial of degree at most d with P(0) = 1 and gives h_0 = 1, and reading the coefficient of t in each basis element, gives exactly a_1 = H_d + sum over i of (-1)^(i-1) h_i / (i C(d,i)). The magnitude equals (i-1)!(d-i)!/d!, unchanged under i to d+1-i, while the sign flips exactly when d is even, so for even d the terms pair and a_1 differs from H_d only through the asymmetry of the h vector; at d = 6 it reads a_1 = 49/20 + (h_1-h_6)/6 - (h_2-h_5)/30 + (h_3-h_4)/60. Every other coefficient is a fixed linear functional of the same vector, so the translation covers the whole statement. Checked against Reeve's tetrahedron, where h = (1,0,r-1,0) gives a_1 = (12-r)/6 and reproduces the known threshold r > 12.
output: A second language for the objective, exact and rank-uniform, and an honest account of what it does and does not buy. It buys the basis the subject's inequalities are actually stated in: Stanley's nonnegativity, Hibi's lower bound, monotonicity and the unimodality results are all statements about h, and the survey literature is organised around them. It does not buy the conjecture, and the identity shows precisely why: a large h_2 alone drives a_1 negative, which is exactly Reeve's tetrahedron, so Ehrhart positivity fails in general and any proof through this route must say what the hive polytopes' h vectors satisfy that a general polytope's do not. Two cautions enter the record with it. The hive polytopes are rational rather than lattice, so h here is a basis change of a polynomial and not the h* vector of a lattice polytope, and the classical inequalities do not apply without an argument that nothing here supplies. And the identity is exact, so it adds no evidence either way by itself. What it changes for the attack is the shape of the target: from the sign of a sum of weighted edge lengths to an asymmetry bound on a vector of six numbers, computable from the polynomials the project already holds.

action: The same entry again, carrying the translation of move 3 from a change of basis to an algebraic invariant, derived in study/h-as-a-hilbert-numerator.md with no computation. Let C be the cone over the hive polytope at height one and S its lattice points, graded by height, so that the degree-t part is tH intersected with the lattice and the Hilbert function is the stretched polynomial. Summing the binomial basis gives sum over t of C(t+d-i, d) z^t = z^i/(1-z)^(d+1), because the term vanishes below t = i and the substitution t = i+s turns it into C(s+d, d). So move 3's expansion is exactly the statement that the generating function of the stretched polynomial is h(z)/(1-z)^(d+1), and the h vector is the numerator of the Hilbert series of the semigroup ring of S.
output: The h vector is an invariant of a ring, not a bookkeeping device, and that gives a sharper target. S is the full set of lattice points of a pointed rational cone, hence a saturated and so normal affine semigroup, so its ring is Cohen-Macaulay by Hochster's theorem; and for a Cohen-Macaulay graded ring generated in degree one the numerator of the Hilbert series over (1-z)^(dimension) is the Hilbert function of an Artinian reduction and has nonnegative coefficients. Generation in degree one is exactly the integer decomposition property of the hive polytope. So if the hive polytopes are integrally closed then their h vectors are nonnegative, which turns a question about individual coefficients into a known kind of question about a well-studied family. What does not follow is the conjecture: Reeve's tetrahedron has h = (1,0,r-1,0), nonnegative for every r, and linear coefficient (12-r)/6, negative for r > 12, so nonnegativity of h is a floor and the target remains move 3's asymmetry inequality, that the even-indexed part of the sum of h_i/(i C(d,i)) does not exceed the harmonic number plus the odd-indexed part. The implication is also one-way: Reeve's tetrahedron has nonnegative h without being integrally closed, so the property is sufficient and not necessary. The first measurable question is now sharp and concerns data the project already holds, and any run for it is gated.

action: The test step of the same entry, approved with eight amendments that cut the proposal from four tests to one. The three dropped: the asymmetry inequality of move 3 is equivalent to the linear coefficient being nonnegative, which the box attack already certified on this data with two independent programs, so testing it can only return a pass; monotonicity is a statement about a nested pair and no pairs were named; Hibi's lower bound needs a lattice polytope with an interior lattice point and no decision hung on it. The one kept is the sign of the h vector, which move 4 makes decisive: a negative entry refutes nonnegativity for the family and, by the contrapositive of move 4, refutes the integer decomposition property for that polytope. deterministic/certified-special-case-check-1 is the box attack's own census script, which already computes every h vector by the alternating sum and was independently checked, with three additions and no other change: the smallest entry, the count of records with a negative entry by index, and the records that have one. Independent checker (check.sh, harness status pass): the summary against the record files and the emptiness of the negative file; an independent h on 590 sampled records computed by solving the triangular system instead of the alternating sum; and a positive control on the detector itself, the synthetic polynomial 1 - 2t + t^2 whose h is (1, -3, 4), so that a census of zero is not the result of a test that never fires.
output: Over 6,855,302 polynomials, 1,334,669 with five parts, 4,217,762 with six and 1,302,871 with seven, no h vector has a negative entry and the smallest entry seen anywhere is zero, in 103 seconds. What that does not mean is stated with it, and it is most of the finding. It does not make the classical inequalities available, because Stanley's theorem gives nonnegative h unconditionally for lattice polytopes, so every record whose hive polytope happens to be a lattice polytope carries no information, and this census cannot separate those from the genuinely rational ones without constructing the polytopes. It does not touch the conjecture either, since Reeve's tetrahedron has nonnegative h and a negative linear coefficient. What it does is remove the cheapest way the route could have died: one negative entry would have ended it and refuted the integer decomposition property for that polytope, and none appeared. The question that now decides the route's value is whether the hive polytopes are integrally closed, which move 4 proves sufficient for nonnegative h, and it is registered in the admission record as needing its own review.

action: A derivation on data already recorded, with no run, written to study/not-integrally-closed.md. If the semigroup of lattice points in the cone over a hive polytope were generated in degree one, then every degree-t element would be a sum of t degree-one elements, so P(t) would be at most the number of multisets of size t from c generators, that is C(t + c - 1, c - 1). Taking c = D + 1, which is exactly the condition h_1 = 0 since h_1 = P(1) - (D+1), the bound is C(t + D, D), whose leading coefficient is one over D factorial, while the leading coefficient of P is the normalized volume over D factorial. So a polytope with h_1 = 0 and normalized volume at least two is not generated in degree one. The sign census of move 5 already carries the count of records with h_1 = 0 by dimension and normalized volume, and the maximum normalized volume among them is two at every length.
output: The question move 5 left as the one that decides this route's value is answered, and the answer is no. The hive polytopes are not all integrally closed: at five parts 304 records have h_1 = 0, dimension four and normalized volume two; at six parts 3,088 in dimension four and 1,098 in dimension five; at seven parts 151, 1,632 and 1,196 in dimensions four, five and six. An explicit one is lam = (17,4,3,2,1), mu = (16,3,2,1), nu = (2,2,1), with five lattice points, normalized volume two and h = (1,0,1,0,0). So the sufficient condition of move 4 is not what produces the nonnegativity the census found, which makes that census result more interesting rather than less: nonnegative h held in all 6,855,302 records although the family fails the property that would have explained it, so either some weaker property is at work or the nonnegativity is a coincidence of the box, and nothing in the attack decides between those. The move also removes an obligation cleanly rather than adding one: the integral-closure question needed no run, no allowance and no review, because the data to answer it was already recorded.

action: A derivation with one citation and no run, written to study/why-h-is-nonnegative.md, answering the question move 6 left. Move 5 found no negative entry in 6,855,302 h vectors and move 6 showed that integral closure, the sufficient condition of move 4, fails for the family, and that the failing polytopes are not lattice polytopes either, having seven vertices and five lattice points. So neither route that would explain nonnegative h applies. The mechanism proposed has two elementary steps and one citation. First, the vector h is determined by the polynomial alone, by the basis change of move 3, so a rational polytope with the same Ehrhart polynomial as a lattice polytope has that polytope's h star vector, and Stanley's theorem gives nonnegativity unconditionally with no integral closure in it. Second, cutting a polytope into half-open pieces and moving them by lattice-preserving affine maps changes no dilate's lattice-point count, so scissors congruence in that sense gives Ehrhart equivalence. Third, Haase and McAllister, Quasi-period collapse and GL_n(Z)-scissors congruence in rational polytopes, arXiv:0709.4070, take up exactly the phenomenon the hive polytopes exhibit; the citation is to the title and the abstract as retrieved on 2026-09-05 and no numbered statement of theirs is relied on.
output: A mechanism that would explain the census, and a cheap test of it that has not been run. If the five-part hive polytopes are lattice-preserving scissors congruent to lattice polytopes then both the period collapse and the nonnegative h follow, and neither integral closure nor lattice vertices are needed. That is consistent with everything the record holds and is not proved here. What makes it worth recording rather than merely plausible is that it is falsifiable on data already held: Ehrhart equivalence to a lattice polytope forces h to satisfy every inequality that h star vectors of lattice polytopes satisfy, and three are standard and computable from the recorded vectors with no polytope construction, Stanley's inequality on partial sums from the bottom against those from the top, Hibi's lower bound that h_1 is at most h_i for i between one and d minus one when h_d is nonzero, and h_d at most h_1. A single record violating one refutes the mechanism for that polytope outright, which would be sharper than the nonnegativity census and reached the same way. What the mechanism does not do is bear on the conjecture: Reeve's tetrahedron is a lattice polytope, satisfies every inequality above, and has a negative linear coefficient for large parameter, so the mechanism would explain the h census and nothing more.
